name: Carlos Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Pennick Eggs, a free-range farm with about thirty-two thousand hens in four big sheds, out past the reservoir. I start at six, walk the sheds, pick up the floor eggs, that's the ones the hens lay on the floor instead of in the nest boxes, check the drinkers and feeders, and take out any birds that have died in the night. Then it's the packing room, watching the grading machine and stacking trays till two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two and a half years. Before that I was twenty-eight years at the bottling plant in Ferris Lane, ending up as a line supervisor. Then they put in a new automated line, and it needed four people instead of eleven, and I was one of the seven. I was fifty-five. My son-in-law knew the Pennick family, and here I am, a beginner again with a bucket of eggs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet in the sheds early, the hens making that low sound, like a room full of people murmuring at church before it starts. What's hard is being told what to do by a twenty-six-year-old, Josh, who's good at the job, and I'm not yet. And the money, Rosa works in the kitchen at the church school, and we manage, but with less than a month in the bank. Every time the van makes a noise, I hold my breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that sounds about right, a useful tool. I use it a bit myself, my son-in-law showed me. I asked it once why the hens in shed three were pecking each other, and it gave me a list of reasons, and one of them was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. I've been automated out once already. If it stays a search engine, I can keep my head down here until I'm sixty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and try to get good, really good, at the sheds, so Josh doesn't have to tell me things twice. I might use the AI thing to read up on hen diseases on Sunday evenings. And I'd keep putting the bit aside for the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A Sunday afternoon kind of feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was the reason for the pecking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Too much light coming in through a broken shutter, the hens got stressed. I found it, told Josh, and he fixed it. The AI got me looking in the right place, but I found the shutter, I'd like that on the record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you were automated out once. How did that day go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They called us in one at a time. The manager had a folder, and he said, Carlos, you've been a great servant to this company. Servant. I've thought about that word a lot since.

S0.say: I'd say a useful tool sounds about right. I use it a bit myself, and it once helped me work out why the hens were pecking each other.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because I've already been automated out once. If it stays a search engine, I can keep my head down here until I'm sixty-seven.
S0.do: Works at getting really good in the sheds so the young manager needn't repeat himself. Reads up on hen diseases with AI on Sunday evenings and keeps saving for the van.
S0.feel: Calm, a Sunday afternoon kind of feeling.
S0.quote: Carlos, you've been a great servant to this company. Servant. I've thought about that word a lot since.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos has lived through automation once and carries the word 'servant' from that day. He uses AI a little, carefully, and wanted credit for finding the broken shutter himself. His goal is simple: keep his head down until pension age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies will do what's best for business, and that's their right. But I'd say a good company keeps a ladder for young people, apprenticeships, because that's how you build loyalty. At the plant, the best supervisors had all started on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, slow change is how I lost my last job, so I don't trust slow. They talked about the new line for six years before it came. By the time it arrived, everyone had stopped worrying, and that's when it got us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This time, I'd watch. I'd ask Mr Pennick, politely, what machines he's thinking about for the sheds over the next few years. I'd learn whatever's coming before it comes, even if it means staying late unpaid. And I'd start putting aside twenty a week, even if it means no takeaway on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like I've seen this film before and know the ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mr Pennick tell you the truth about his plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. He's an old-fashioned man, he goes to our church, he'd tell me straight if I asked straight. The trouble last time was that nobody asked. I won't make that mistake again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twenty a week with under a month saved. What else gives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Friday takeaway, which Rosa will mind, and my football subscription on the television. Small things. But twenty a week is a thousand a year, and a thousand is a van repair.

S1.say: I'd say companies will do what's best for business, which is their right, but a good company keeps apprenticeships as a ladder for young people. It builds loyalty.
S1.think: I don't trust slow change, because that's how I lost my last job. People stopped worrying just before the new line arrived.
S1.do: Asks the farm owner directly what machines he plans for the sheds and learns them early, even unpaid. Saves twenty a week by dropping the Friday takeaway and his football subscription.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like watching a film whose ending he already knows.
S1.quote: By the time it arrived, everyone had stopped worrying, and that's when it got us.
S1.fieldNote: Interesting reversal: for him, slow change is the dangerous kind, because it lulls people. He respects business decisions but wants employers to keep ladders for the young. His steady streak shows in the habit of asking straight this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hard on the office people, but this country has been through changes before, and people adapt. I'd say families have to pull together, and I'd be wary of politicians promising to fix everything with other people's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's not my world, but it is my daughter's. Sofia does the accounts for a car dealership, and that's routine office work if anything is. Her husband, the one who got me this job, sells insurance. Both of them at once would be a real blow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sofia and Mark they can lean on us for anything but money, because there isn't any. Rosa would mind the grandchildren after school. I'd talk to Mr Pennick about whether there's packing work for Sofia if it came to it, though it pays half what she earns now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, for them. It's a strange thing to be the one with the safe job in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said be wary of politicians spending other people's money. If Sofia needed help, would you want her to take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know how that sounds. I'd want her to take what she's paid in for. That's not a handout, that's insurance she bought. It's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Sofia really pack eggs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say over my dead body, Dad. Then she'd come and do a week and be faster than me by Thursday. She's always been quicker than me.

S2.say: I'd say it's hard on office people, but the country has adapted before and families must pull together. I'd be wary of politicians fixing everything with other people's money.
S2.think: It's not my world, but it is my daughter's. She does accounts for a car dealership and her husband sells insurance, so both could be hit at once.
S2.do: Offers his daughter's family everything but money, with his wife minding the grandchildren after school. Asks the farm owner about packing work for his daughter if needed.
S2.feel: Anxious for his daughter's family, and strange to be the one with the safe job.
S2.quote: I'd want her to take what she's paid in for. That's not a handout, that's insurance she bought.
S2.fieldNote: When I pressed on the gap between his views and his daughter's needs, he drew a clear line between handouts and benefits people paid into. His support is time and childcare, not money. He was warm and slightly rueful about his daughter being quicker than him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built the companies deserve the gains, but they'd be wise to share some with their workers, or there'll be trouble. And I'd say the crisis is what happens when people stop trusting each other. Church, family, community, that's what holds things together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, eggs are eggs. People eat them whether shares go up or down, and nobody's sending AI into a hen shed in this picture. But Rosa and I rent, and if house prices boom, I know what happens to rents. Our landlord has already hinted twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the landlord and offer to sign a longer lease now, in return for keeping the rent where it is. I'd ask Mr Pennick about overtime, there's always weekend packing before Easter and Christmas. And I'd go to church and pray for some calm in the country, because I'd be worried for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the rent and the country, steady about the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your landlord, word for word?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Mr Okafor, I've never been late, not once in nine years, and I fix things myself and don't bother you. Keep it as it is, and I'll sign for three years. He's a businessman, he'd see the sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the crisis in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know enough to blame anyone in particular. People in a hurry, on all sides. I'd blame the shouting more than the machines.

S3.say: I'd say the builders of companies deserve the gains but would be wise to share some with workers. Church, family and community hold things together when trust breaks.
S3.think: Eggs are eggs, and nobody's sending AI into a hen shed in this picture. But we rent, and in a house boom our landlord, who has already hinted twice, will raise it.
S3.do: Offers his landlord a three-year lease in return for freezing the rent. Asks for weekend overtime packing before Easter and Christmas and goes to church to pray for calm.
S3.feel: Uneasy about the rent and the country, steady about the job.
S3.quote: I'd blame the shouting more than the machines.
S3.fieldNote: He was candid that he doesn't know enough to blame anyone specific, and blamed the shouting. His threat in this picture is rent, and his answer was a businesslike deal with the landlord. Faith and community came through as his idea of what holds things together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can't stop progress, but a decent business owes its people a proper warning and a fair send-off. I'd say men like me, who've been through this once, should be listened to, because we know how it goes. I'd say it at church and to Mr Pennick directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the bottling plant all over again, only worse, because I'm fifty-eight, not fifty-five. There are already machines that crawl around sheds picking up floor eggs, Josh showed me a video. Shed work, packing, it's all exactly what robots are built for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Pennick to let me run or watch the new machines, because I supervised an automated line for years, I know how they break. I'd ask the church for any leads, and Rosa would ask at the school. We'd sell the van and get something cheaper, and I'd start looking at caretaker jobs, but I know those may be going too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The second time is worse, because you know exactly what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the second time is worse. What's the moment you'd dread most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The folder. The manager with the folder, saying my name kindly. If Mr Pennick has to do it, I'd rather he just told me in the yard, man to man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of you that thinks you could do well in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small part. I know lines and machines and how they jam, Josh doesn't. If Mr Pennick is smart, he keeps one old man who's seen a machine fail at three in the morning. I'd make that case. Whether he listens, I don't know.

S4.say: I'd say we can't stop progress, but a decent business owes its people warning and a fair send-off. People who've been through it before should be listened to.
S4.think: It's the bottling plant again, only worse at fifty-eight. Machines already pick up floor eggs, and shed and packing work is exactly what robots are built for.
S4.do: Asks the farm owner to let him run or watch the new machines, drawing on his years supervising an automated line. Seeks leads through church and his wife's school, sells the van for something cheaper and looks at caretaker work.
S4.feel: Alarmed. The second time is worse because he knows exactly what's coming.
S4.quote: I'd rather he just told me in the yard, man to man.
S4.fieldNote: His past made this picture vivid: he could picture the folder and the kind voice. Still, he found a case for himself as someone who's seen automated lines fail. He wanted dignity in how the news is delivered as much as he wanted to keep the job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one. I've been on the wrong end of a machine once, and I know how long it takes to get back up at my age. What would help is a business that tells you a year ahead and keeps one or two experienced people on to mind the machines. And apprenticeships for the young, so it's not just old men like me and nobody behind us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how it ends at home. When I lost the plant job, I didn't tell Rosa for two days. I drove around. I'd want people to know that men like me hide it, and somebody should notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you for saying that. Anything else?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No. Only that the hens will be fine whatever happens. They always are.

headlineQuote: The folder. The manager with the folder, saying my name kindly.
portrait: Carlos Chen is 58 and has worked for two and a half years at a 32,000-hen free-range egg farm, collecting floor eggs and watching the grading machine, after an automated line cost him his supervisor job at a bottling plant at 55. He and his wife Rosa, a church school cook, rent and have less than a month saved, and he uses AI now and then for hen problems. He distrusts slow change because that is how he was caught out before, worries for his daughter's office job, and frames help as family, church and benefits people paid into rather than handouts. In the robot picture he is alarmed at being automated twice, but argues his experience with machine lines could make him worth keeping.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries him most, because he has been replaced by a machine once and knows how hard the second time would be at his age.
whatWouldHelp: A year's warning, keeping one or two experienced people to mind the machines, and apprenticeships for the young. He also wants someone to notice men who hide job loss from their families.
